region_note: Written for irrigated rice-wheat farms of central-southern Punjab (about 230 m, semi-arid, 550-650 mm of rain, three quarters of it in July-September). Crop calendars follow PAU's Package of Practices. Do not reuse elsewhere without local review.

equipment.label: Seed drill, zero-till drill or Happy Seeder

market.label: Only crops with assured buying (MSP procurement)
Open to mandi crops with price risk

references.FAO56: Allen, R.G., Pereira, L.S., Raes, D., Smith, M. (1998). Crop evapotranspiration. FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper 56 (Tables 11, 12, 17, 22).
references.FAO33: Doorenbos, J., Kassam, A.H. (1979). Yield response to water. FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper 33; updated in Steduto et al. (2012), FAO Paper 66.
references.FAO29: Ayers, R.S., Westcot, D.W. (1985). Water quality for agriculture. FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper 29, Table 4 (crop salt tolerance).
references.PAU: Punjab Agricultural University, Ludhiana. Package of Practices for Crops of Punjab: Kharif and Rabi (published every year). Sowing windows, durations and irrigation numbers.
references.HUMPHREYS: Humphreys, E. et al. (2010). Halting the groundwater decline in north-west India: which crop technologies will be winners? Advances in Agronomy 109: 155-217. (Only lower ET is a real saving; water that percolates from paddy largely returns to the aquifer.)
references.ACT2009: The Punjab Preservation of Subsoil Water Act, 2009: paddy nursery and transplanting dates are fixed by notification each year (transplanting from mid-June), to move the crop away from the hottest, driest weeks.
references.RODELL: Rodell, M., Velicogna, I., Famiglietti, J.S. (2009). Satellite-based estimates of groundwater depletion in India. Nature 460: 999-1002. (GRACE: about 4 cm of water a year lost across Rajasthan, Punjab and Haryana, 2002-2008.)
references.CGWB: Central Ground Water Board, Dynamic Ground Water Resources of India (periodic assessments): most blocks of Sangrur and Barnala districts are classed over-exploited.
references.SARE: Clark, A. (ed.) (2007). Managing Cover Crops Profitably, 3rd edition. SARE Handbook 9 (legume nitrogen).
references.CA: Jat, M.L. et al. and CIMMYT-ICAR work on conservation agriculture in the rice-wheat and maize-wheat systems of north-west India (zero tillage, residue retention with the Happy Seeder, summer mungbean).
references.PROJECT: Class score assigned by this project from the general agronomy cited alongside it; not locally calibrated.

water.label: Save water
water.plain: Less water lost from the field across the whole rotation.

cover.label: Keep soil covered
cover.plain: Crop or residue on the ground when wind and heavy rain arrive.

nitrogen.label: Nitrogen from legumes
nitrogen.plain: Nitrogen fixed by pulses and used by the next crop.

organic_matter.label: Build organic matter
organic_matter.plain: Roots and residue returned to the soil, not burnt; less puddling.

pest_break.label: Break pest cycles
pest_break.plain: Different plant families instead of the same two crops every year.

income.label: Income and assured sale
income.plain: Crop value relative to rice-wheat, given your water and how you sell.

resilience.label: Heat and dry-spell resilience
resilience.plain: Crops that cope with hot spells and short water.

feasibility.label: Easy to carry out
feasibility.plain: Fits your season, machinery and experience.

why.kc: FAO56 Table 12: rice Kc 1.05 initial, 1.20 mid-season, 0.90-0.60 late. June is counted at about half because transplanting starts from mid-June (ACT2009).
why.cover: Standing water and canopy from July to September; after combine harvest the loose straw is usually burnt or removed, leaving the soil nearly bare in late October-November (PROJECT).
why.om_score: Puddling breaks soil structure every year and most straw is burnt or removed (CA; PROJECT).
why.drought_tolerance: The most water-sensitive cereal: yield falls faster than water (Ky about 1.2, FAO33).
why.value_score: With wheat this makes up the reference income (rice 0.55 + wheat 0.45 = 1.0). Procured at the minimum support price: an assured sale.
why.extra_water_mm: On top of what the crop transpires, puddling and keeping the field flooded take roughly 700-1,000 mm more pumping. Most of that seeps back to the aquifer, so it costs pumping and electricity rather than groundwater (HUMPHREYS). It is shown in the app but not counted in the water score.

why.kc: FAO56 Table 12: winter wheat Kc 0.4-0.7 initial, 1.15 mid-season, 0.25-0.4 at harvest; sown in November, harvested mid-April (PAU).
why.cover: Bare seedbed in November unless sown into rice residue; full canopy January-March; stubble after April.
why.heat_limit_c: Heat above about 32 °C during grain filling in March shrivels the grain ('terminal heat'); this is the crop's main climate risk here (PAU).
why.om_score: Fibrous roots; the straw is taken off as fodder.
why.value_score: Reference income together with rice; procured at the minimum support price.

why.kc: FAO56 Table 12: maize (grain) Kc 0.3 initial, 1.20 mid-season, 0.35-0.6 late; sown mid-June to early July (PAU). No puddling and no standing water.
why.om_score: More stalk and root left than rice, with no puddling (CA).
why.drought_tolerance: Very sensitive to dry spells at tasselling and silking (Ky 1.25, FAO33); it also suffers from waterlogging after heavy monsoon rain.
why.value_score: A support price is announced but little is bought at it; prices in the mandi swing, and grain has to be dried (PROJECT class score; no prices in this tool).
why.establishment_risk: Stands are easily lost to waterlogging or stray cattle; fall armyworm has been a pest since 2018 (PAU).

why.kc: FAO56 Table 12: cotton Kc 0.35 initial, 1.15-1.20 mid-season, 0.70-0.50 late; sown late April-May, picked October-November (PAU).
why.drought_tolerance: Deep taproot; yield falls less than water (Ky 0.85, FAO33).
why.establishment_risk: Whitefly and pink bollworm have caused repeated crop failures in the cotton belt; this is the crop's defining risk (PAU).
why.value_score: Can match paddy in a good year, but yields and prices swing widely; bought by the Cotton Corporation of India and private traders.

why.kc: FAO56 Table 12: green gram Kc 0.4 initial, 1.05 mid-season, 0.60-0.35 late. Short-duration varieties fit between wheat harvest and paddy transplanting (PAU). April and June are part months.
why.n_score: A legume that fixes nitrogen; ploughing in the residue after picking the pods returns roughly 25-50 kg N/ha (SARE; CA).
why.value_score: A small extra crop; a support price exists but buying at it has been patchy.
why.establishment_risk: Pre-monsoon rain at maturity spoils the grain, and the crop needs 3-4 irrigations in the hottest weeks of the year (PAU).
why.drought_tolerance: Grown in May-June, when the weather's water demand is at its yearly peak.

why.kc: FAO56 Table 12: chickpea Kc 0.4 initial, 1.00 mid-season, 0.35 late; sown late October, harvested late March (PAU).
why.n_score: A legume: fixes its own nitrogen and leaves some for the next crop (SARE).
why.drought_tolerance: Needs only one or two irrigations; too much water or winter rain brings wilt and blight (PAU).
why.value_score: Lower and less certain yield than wheat; frost in January and pod borer are the main losses (PROJECT class score).

rice_wheat.name: Rice-wheat every year
rice_wheat.summary: Transplanted paddy from mid-June, then wheat from November. What most farms here grow.
benefits: Both crops are bought at the minimum support price: the surest income available.
Machinery, labour, inputs and know-how are all in place.
High and stable yields under assured irrigation.
risks: The highest water use of the options here, in a district whose groundwater is classed over-exploited.
Three weeks between paddy harvest and wheat sowing push farmers to burn the straw.
Two cereals every year: weeds such as Phalaris, and soil that hardens under puddling.
Wheat is exposed to March heat; late sowing after paddy makes it worse.
info_gaps: Your tubewell depth, discharge and how fast the water level is falling.
Whether you burn, remove or keep the paddy straw.
verify: Ask the block agriculture office for the groundwater category of your block.
Ask PAU or the KVK about short-duration paddy varieties and the Happy Seeder for sowing wheat into straw.

rice_wheat_moong.name: Rice-wheat with summer moong
rice_wheat_moong.summary: The same rice and wheat, with a 60-day moong crop in April-June between them.
benefits: Adds a legume: some nitrogen for the paddy and a third plant family.
Covers the soil in the hot, windy weeks of May.
A little extra income without giving up rice or wheat.
risks: Moong needs 3-4 irrigations in the hottest part of the year: this option uses MORE water, not less.
Rain at maturity in June can ruin the grain.
Leaves very little time before paddy transplanting.
info_gaps: Whether moong was bought at the support price in your mandi last season.
Whitefly and yellow mosaic pressure in your village.
verify: Check with the KVK which short-duration variety and sowing date fit after your wheat harvest.
Ask whether procurement of moong is planned this year.

maize_wheat_moong.name: Maize instead of paddy, with wheat and summer moong
maize_wheat_moong.summary: Kharif maize replaces paddy; wheat follows; summer moong fills April-June.
benefits: Maize transpires less than paddy and needs no puddling or standing water: far less pumping.
No paddy straw to burn; wheat can be sown on time.
Soil structure recovers without puddling, and a legume is added.
risks: Maize has no assured buyer at the support price: income depends on the mandi price.
Maize fails if the field floods after heavy monsoon rain, or dries at tasselling.
Needs a planter, and the grain must be dried before sale.
info_gaps: Maize price and buyers near you (starch mills, poultry feed, ethanol plants).
Whether your fields drain well enough for maize in a wet July.
verify: Ask about the state's crop-diversification incentive for moving out of paddy.
Talk to a neighbour who grows kharif maize about drainage and fall armyworm.
Line up a buyer or a dryer before sowing.

cotton_wheat.name: Cotton-wheat
cotton_wheat.summary: Bt cotton from May to November, then late-sown wheat. The rotation of Punjab's south-west.
benefits: A deep-rooted crop from a different family; no puddling.
Tolerates salty water and soil better than paddy or maize.
Can earn as much as paddy in a good year.
risks: Whitefly and pink bollworm have wiped out crops in recent years: the largest risk of any option here.
Wheat is sown late after the last picking, which exposes it more to March heat.
Picking needs a lot of labour.
info_gaps: Pest pressure in your block over the last three seasons.
Whether heavier soils here suit cotton; it prefers lighter, well-drained land.
verify: Ask the agriculture department for this year's recommended Bt hybrids and the pest advisory.
Check canal or tubewell water quality if salinity is suspected.

alternate_paddy.name: Paddy every other year
alternate_paddy.summary: Rice-wheat one year; maize, gram and summer moong the next.
benefits: Halves the paddy area while keeping an assured crop every year.
Two legumes in two years and four plant groups.
The field is puddled only every second year.
risks: Gram and maize have less certain yields and prices than wheat and paddy.
More crops to learn and more sowing dates to hit.
Gram dislikes heavy, wet soil and frost.
info_gaps: Local prices for maize and gram.
Whether your soil is light enough for gram.
verify: Try it on a part of the farm first.
Ask PAU extension which gram and maize varieties suit your block.

always_verify: Groundwater category of your block and the depth of water in your own tubewell.
A soil health card test (organic carbon, pH, salinity, nutrients).
This season's minimum support prices and which crops are actually being procured.
Sowing windows and varieties in the current PAU Package of Practices.
